# Datasets and codebook {#datasets}

Three kinds of data enter this book: crease-pattern manifolds generated on
demand, one precomputed result table, and one external dataset used once, in
Chapter \@ref(application). Symbols referred to below are defined in Appendix
\@ref(notation).

## Generated data {-}

All crease-pattern manifolds are generated, not collected. Every dataset in
Parts I–III is reproducible from a pattern specification, a fold angle, a
sample size, a noise specification, and a seed.

### Specification schema {-}

Those five things are the whole record. Nothing else about a generated dataset
is free to vary, and nothing else needs to be stored: the specification *is* the
data.

| Field | Type | Domain | Grid value | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `pattern` | character | `"miura"`, `"yoshimura"`, `"waterbomb"` | all three | Pattern family; selects the constructor |
| `n_rows`, `n_cols` | integer | $\ge 1$ | `6`, `6` | Unit cells per axis. All three constructors take these |
| `a`, `b` | double | $> 0$ | `1`, `1` | Unit-cell edge lengths. All three constructors take these |
| `alpha` | double | $(0, \pi/2)$ rad | `pi/3` | Miura-ori unit-cell acute angle. `miura_ori()` only; sets the row shear $b/\tan\alpha$ of the *flat* pattern |
| `theta` | double | $[0, \pi/2)$ rad | `seq(0, 1.4, by = 0.1)` | Fold angle. The difficulty parameter |
| `n` | integer | $\ge 100$ | `800` | Sample size |
| `noise$type` | character | `"none"`, `"ambient"`, `"manifold"`, `"outlier"` | `none`, `ambient`, `outlier` | Which channel the noise perturbs |
| `noise$sd` | double | $\ge 0$ | `0`, `0.02`, `0.05` | Noise scale $\sigma$. One magnitude; the type decides what it moves. Under `"outlier"` a fixed 2% of rows are displaced by $10\sigma$ |
| `seed` | integer | any | `BENCH_SEEDS` $= 1001\ldots1020$ | RNG seed for the replicate |
| `D` | integer | $\ge 3$ | `3` (unlifted) | Ambient dimension after `lift()` |

The fold angle is bounded above by $\pi/2$, exclusive, and that bound is the
same for every pattern — there is no per-family maximum and no `theta_max()`.
Fold angles are therefore reported on one absolute scale, in radians, with no
normalisation step and nothing to rescale between families.

### Implementation note {-}

The `pattern` field selects a *flat crease pattern*. In the `foldbench` version
shipped alongside this book the three constructors build genuinely different
flat patterns — different vertices, different crease sets, different
mountain/valley assignments — but `fold()` and `sample_manifold()` drive all of
them along the same one-parameter accordion path, so the sampled manifolds
differ only in their bounding boxes. `alpha` likewise shapes the flat unit cell
and not the folded geometry. The accordion is a genuine isometry and the ground
truth is exact, so nothing in Parts I–III is invalidated; but a reader analysing
the committed grid should not read the `pattern` factor as three distinct folded
geometries. Differentiating the fold by family is open work, recorded here
rather than in a chapter because it is a property of the data, not of an
argument.

### Return value {-}

`sample_manifold()` returns a list with four elements. This is the unit of
analysis everywhere in Parts I–III.

| Element | Type | Shape | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `X` | double matrix | $n \times 3$, or $n \times D$ after `lift()` | Ambient sample. The only thing a method under test is allowed to see |
| `U` | double matrix | $n \times 2$ | True unfolding of the same $n$ points. The answer key |
| `facet` | integer vector | length $n$ | Facet index of each point; a categorical covariate, never an input to a method |
| `theta` | double | scalar | The fold angle used, carried for provenance |

`X` and `U` are row-aligned: row $i$ of `U` is the flat-sheet coordinate of the
point in row $i$ of `X`. That alignment is what makes $\mathrm{RMSE}_{\mathrm{P}}$
computable and is the single reason this benchmark exists.

```{r datasets-spec-example}
spec <- list(
  pattern = "miura", n_rows = 6L, n_cols = 6L, a = 1, b = 1, alpha = pi / 3,
  theta   = 0.8,
  n       = 800L,
  noise   = list(type = "ambient", sd = 0.02),
  seed    = 1001L
)

pat <- miura_ori(spec$n_rows, spec$n_cols, a = spec$a, b = spec$b,
                 alpha = spec$alpha)

# sample_manifold() takes the pattern and the angle, not a pre-folded object.
mfd <- sample_manifold(pat, theta = spec$theta, n = spec$n,
                       noise = spec$noise, seed = spec$seed)

str(mfd)          # list of two: X (n x 3 ambient) and truth (n x 2 answer key)
```

### Determinism {-}

A specification reproduces a dataset bit for bit given the same `foldbench`
version and the same R RNG. R changed its default sampling algorithm in 3.6.0;
the book assumes `RNGkind(sample.kind = "Rejection")`, the post-3.6.0 default,
and results generated under the older `"Rounding"` rule will not match. No
generated dataset is committed to the repository. Reproducing a figure means
re-running its specification, not downloading a file.

## Precomputed results {-}

`data/processed/benchmark-grid.rds` — the Chapter \@ref(results) grid.
Provenance: `scripts/run-benchmark-grid.R`.

The grid is the one exception to the rule above: it takes hours to compute, so
it is generated once, committed, and read at render time. The script is kept as
the provenance record rather than run during the build.

### Columns {-}

`scripts/run-benchmark-grid.R` writes one row per
(pattern, fold angle, noise, seed, method), with **one column per metric**. The
layout is wide, not long: the script builds each row from a single
`sample_manifold()` draw and scores all four metrics against that same draw, so
the metrics share a row by construction. Chapter \@ref(evaluation), which faces
the metrics against each other, reshapes to long itself rather than the file
being stored that way.

| Column | Type | Levels or range | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `pattern` | character, 3 levels | `miura`, `yoshimura`, `waterbomb` | Pattern family |
| `theta` | double | $[0, 1.4]$ rad on the committed grid | Fold angle |
| `noise` | character, 3 levels | `none`, `ambient`, `outlier` | Noise condition; see the specification table above |
| `seed` | integer | `1001`–`1020` | Replicate identifier; equals the seed passed to `sample_manifold()` |
| `method` | character, 5 levels | `pca`, `mds`, `isomap`, `tsne`, `umap` | Embedding method, at the hyperparameters fixed in its own chapter |
| `rmse` | double | $[0, \infty)$, lower better, `NA` permitted | `reconstruction_error(Y, truth)` — Procrustes-aligned RMSE against the answer key |
| `trust` | double | $[0, 1]$, higher better, `NA` permitted | `trustworthiness(X, Y, k = 10)` |
| `cont` | double | $[0, 1]$, higher better, `NA` permitted | `continuity(X, Y, k = 10)` |
| `knn` | double | $[0, 1]$, higher better, `NA` permitted | `knn_preservation(X, Y, k = 10)` |

`rmse` is the only column compared against the truth; `trust`, `cont` and `knn`
are all computed against the ambient sample `X`. That asymmetry is the subject of
Chapter \@ref(evaluation).

`NA` in a metric column is a result, not a gap. A method that could not embed a
configuration at all — Isomap on a k-NN graph that has fallen into
disconnected components, most often — records `NA` across all four metric
columns rather than being dropped. Dropping it would silently bias every curve upward by removing
exactly the hard configurations the benchmark exists to expose. Count the `NA`s
before averaging over anything.

The Chapter \@ref(autoencoders) autoencoder is absent from the committed grid.
It is the one method whose result depends on a training run rather than a
closed-form or fixed-iteration procedure, and the render workflow excludes
`torch` from the restored library; its figures come from a recorded run
documented in that chapter instead of from this file.

Kruskal stress is not in the committed grid. `foldbench` does not export it; it
is defined where it is used, in Chapter \@ref(evaluation), and computed there
from the stored embeddings rather than carried as a column here.

The full cell key is therefore (`pattern`, `theta`, `noise`, `seed`, `method`).
Note that `pattern` carries far less information than its three levels suggest:
the folding stage does not read the crease pattern, so the three families differ
in their flat geometry but fold alike. Chapter \@ref(benchmarks) states the
consequence. Treat differences across `pattern` as near-replicates, not as a
family effect.

The committed grid carries the first four. `kruskal_stress` is computed on
demand in Chapter \@ref(evaluation), where the question is how the metrics
relate to each other rather than how the methods rank.

The last column is the point of the table. Exactly one of the five metrics knows
the answer. The other four are the metrics the field actually uses.

```{r datasets-read-grid}
grid <- readRDS("data/processed/benchmark-grid.rds")
str(grid)
table(grid$method, grid$metric)
```

Neighbourhood size is fixed at $k = 10$ across the committed grid, so `k` is not
a column. Chapter \@ref(evaluation) varies it separately and reports the
sensitivity; the grid deliberately does not, because a metric that changes its
verdict with $k$ is a finding about the metric, not a factor to average over.

## External data {-}

One external dataset is used, once, in Chapter \@ref(application). It is not
part of the benchmark. Its role is to answer whether a benchmark-guided method
choice survives contact with data that has no answer key.

### Selection criteria {-}

The dataset was chosen against five requirements, stated here because they
matter more than the particular choice:

1. **Openly licensed and redistributable.** No controlled access, no data-use
   agreement, no registration wall. A reader must be able to re-run the chapter
   from a clean clone.
2. **Version-pinned.** A fixed processed release with a stable file name and a
   recorded checksum, not a moving "latest" endpoint.
3. **Small.** Processable on a laptop in minutes, so the chapter is checkable
   rather than merely readable.
4. **An unambiguous field default.** The chapter compares a benchmark-guided
   choice against the field-default choice, which requires that the field
   default be published and uncontested for this dataset rather than invented
   for the comparison.
5. **Recognisable.** The reader should already have seen the standard embedding
   of these data, so that a difference is legible as a difference.

### Primary dataset {-}

**3k PBMCs from a Healthy Donor**, 10x Genomics.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Source | 10x Genomics public datasets, <https://www.10xgenomics.com/datasets/3-k-pbm-cs-from-a-healthy-donor-1-standard-1-1-0> |
| Version | Cell Ranger 1.1.0 processed release; transcriptome reference `hg19` |
| Assay | Chromium Single Cell 3′, Illumina NextSeq 500 |
| Accession | None. The dataset is distributed by 10x Genomics directly and has no INSDC or GEO accession. It is identified by the dataset page above plus the file name and checksum below |
| File | `pbmc3k_filtered_gene_bc_matrices.tar.gz`, from <https://cf.10xgenomics.com/samples/cell/pbmc3k/pbmc3k_filtered_gene_bc_matrices.tar.gz> |
| Contents | Filtered gene–barcode matrix, 32,738 genes $\times$ 2,700 barcodes, Matrix Market triplet format |
| Licence | Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) |

The absence of an accession is worth stating plainly rather than papering over
with a plausible-looking identifier. Vendor-hosted datasets are pinned by URL,
file name and checksum; that is the whole provenance chain, and it is weaker
than a repository accession. Record the SHA-256 of the downloaded archive in
`GENERATION_LOG.md` on first use and check it on every subsequent run.

### Preprocessing {-}

The pipeline below is the published Seurat guided-clustering workflow for this
dataset, unmodified. It is used unmodified on purpose: it is the field default
that Chapter \@ref(application) measures against, so changing it would remove
the comparison.

1. Download the archive into `data/raw/pbmc3k/` and untar. Raw data is not
   committed; the download is scripted and checksummed.
2. Read `filtered_gene_bc_matrices/hg19/` with `Seurat::Read10X()`, giving a
   32,738 $\times$ 2,700 sparse count matrix.
3. Gene filter: retain genes detected in at least 3 cells. 13,714 genes remain.
4. Cell QC: retain cells with between 200 and 2,500 detected genes and under
   5% of UMIs from mitochondrial genes (symbols matching `^MT-`). 2,638 cells
   remain.
5. Normalise: scale each cell to 10,000 UMI, then $\log(1 + x)$.
6. Feature selection: the 2,000 most variable genes under the
   variance-stabilising transform.
7. Centre each retained gene and scale to unit variance, clipping at 10
   standard deviations.
8. PCA on the scaled matrix; retain the first 50 components.

Step 8 produces a 2,638 $\times$ 50 matrix. That matrix is $X$ for Chapter
\@ref(application) — the ambient sample every method is given, exactly
analogous to a crease-pattern sample lifted to $D = 50$.

```{r datasets-pbmc-preprocess}
counts <- Seurat::Read10X("data/raw/pbmc3k/filtered_gene_bc_matrices/hg19")

pbmc <- Seurat::CreateSeuratObject(counts, min.cells = 3, min.features = 200)
pbmc[["percent.mt"]] <- Seurat::PercentageFeatureSet(pbmc, pattern = "^MT-")
pbmc <- subset(pbmc, subset = nFeature_RNA < 2500 & percent.mt < 5)

pbmc <- Seurat::NormalizeData(pbmc)
pbmc <- Seurat::FindVariableFeatures(pbmc, selection.method = "vst",
                                     nfeatures = 2000)
pbmc <- Seurat::ScaleData(pbmc, features = Seurat::VariableFeatures(pbmc))
pbmc <- Seurat::RunPCA(pbmc, npcs = 50)

X <- Seurat::Embeddings(pbmc, "pca")   # 2638 x 50 — the ambient sample
```

### Labels {-}

The nine populations conventionally reported for these cells — naive CD4 T,
memory CD4 T, CD14+ monocytes, B, CD8 T, FCGR3A+ monocytes, NK, dendritic
cells, platelets — are marker-based annotations assigned after clustering.
They are a useful reference and they are not ground truth. Nothing in Chapter
\@ref(application) treats them as $U$.

### What this dataset can and cannot show {-}

No $U$ exists for real data, so $\mathrm{RMSE}_{\mathrm{P}}$ is undefined here.
Only the relative metrics — $T_k$, $C_k$, $P_k$, $\sigma_1$ — can be computed,
and Chapter \@ref(evaluation) has already established how optimistic each of
them is and in which direction. The benchmark's job in Chapter
\@ref(application) is therefore to *supply* the method and its hyperparameters,
not to score the outcome. A benchmark that could score the outcome would not
need the benchmark.

The geometry is also a mismatch worth naming. PBMCs form well-separated discrete
populations; a crease pattern is a connected continuum. A differentiation
trajectory would be the closer analogue of a folded sheet, and the trade against
criterion 4 above — an uncontested field default — went the other way.

### Alternates considered {-}

Two datasets meet criteria 1–3 and 5, have continuous rather than clustered
geometry, and were set aside only on criterion 4:

- **Mouse myeloid progenitors**, Paul and colleagues (2015), GEO accession
  `GSE72857`. Roughly 2,730 cells after the authors' filtering, spanning a
  continuous differentiation topology with seven fates. The closest published
  analogue to a folded sheet in this list.
- **Mouse cortex and hippocampus**, GEO accession `GSE60361`, 3,005 cells
  [@zeisel2015cortex]. Discrete cell types, but a long enough analysis history
  that a field default is arguable.

Both are hosted on GEO, which is openly downloadable but does not attach an
explicit reuse licence to deposits; terms follow the depositing publication.
The 10x release carries CC BY 4.0 in writing, which is why it is the primary.
